text: Why does fifty pounds on the cable machine feel so much lighter? Let's take one apart.
Steel plates ride up and down two guide rods. The selector pin decides how many plates you lift.
A steel cable runs from the stack, over a chain of pulleys, out to your handle.
Tie the cable straight to the stack, and it's one to one. Fifty on the pin, fifty in your hand.
But many machines hang the stack from a movable pulley. Now two strands of cable share the weight.
Each strand carries half, so your hand feels about twenty-five pounds. The price? Pull the handle two feet, and the stack rises one.
Force times distance stays the same. Some machines go four to one: a quarter of the force, four times the travel.
Then, reality. Each pulley loses a few percent to friction. Lifting, it adds to the load. Lowering, it helps you.
The steel cable barely stretches, about a millimeter here, so the load hits instantly, not springy.
So the label says fifty. Your hands feel about twenty-five: closer to thirty pulling, twenty letting go.
What should we take apart next?
Congrats! You've discovered the cable machine.
